name: Feathered hair

lead: Feathered hair is a layered hairstyle of the 1970s and early 1980s, designed for straight hair, with a side or center part and the sides brushed back so the layers resemble feathers. It was popularised by Farrah Fawcett's role in Charlie's Angels.
It helps looks by adding volume and movement and framing the face with soft layers. Styles with the same layered structure keep returning in men's and women's fashion.

paras: A stylist cuts layers of different lengths and texturizes the ends. Wearers then blow-dry, brush or curl the sides back or outward to create the flip or wing shape. Grokipedia credits stylists including Allan Edwards, José Eber and Hugh York with pioneering the technique, though the origin is debated.
Hair damage from frequent heat styling is the usual concern with blow-drying and curling. The look depends on hair texture and cut quality.

angle.text: Layering and blow-drying add volume and movement, and the swept-back sides frame the face. People wear it for a retro, voluminous look.

lead: Feathered hair is a layered hairstyle popular in the 1970s and early 1980s, designed for straight hair, with a side or center part and sides brushed back to resemble bird feathers.[1]

It improves appearance by adding movement and volume and framing the face. Wikipedia lists wearers including Farrah Fawcett as Jill Munroe in Charlie's Angels, Jeff Conaway, Dorothy Hamill, Diana, Princess of Wales, John Travolta and Rob Lowe.[1]

Grokipedia says the origin is debated: stylist Allan Edwards claimed to have invented the blow curl method in 1974, while José Eber and Hugh York are also named, and the shag created by Paul McGregor for Jane Fonda around 1970 to 1971 is cited as a precursor.[2] Grokipedia also reports that the 1976 Charlie's Angels poster of Fawcett sold more than 12 million copies;[2] this is AI-generated and unverified. No studies examine the style.

paras: The cut is layered, with sides brushed back and a side or center part.[1] Grokipedia describes ends texturized to look light and often flipped or curled outward around the face.[2]

The origin is disputed; stylists Allan Edwards, José Eber and Hugh York are named in Grokipedia, along with Paul McGregor's shag.[2] The style rose to wide popularity in the early 1970s and spread across the US and Europe through salons and magazines.[1][2] Grokipedia also notes Stevie Nicks and Joan Jett as musicians whose versions of the look circulated.[2]
No studies found. PubMed hits for the phrase concern feathered hair sensilla in lobsters, which are unrelated.
Wikipedia's reference list includes a Hair.com article titled "Feathered Hair Is Back," indicating periodic revivals.[1]

timeline.event: Farrah Fawcett's Charlie's Angels poster cements the look.[2]
